To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) we have introduced a new method for WSD based on a combination of two sense-aware lexical networks, (2) we have shown that the combination of the two networks improves WSD performance, and (3) we have shown, using two standard WSD benchmarks, that the combination of our method with a corpus-based distributional semantic network improves WSD performance over a method based on the distributional semantic network alone.
our approach (1) outperforms a model based solely the lexical resource; and (2) achieves comparable or better results to three state-of-the-art hybrid systems that also make use of corpora.

(1) we have introduced a new unsupervised method for knowledge-based word sense discrimination based on the integration of a manually constructed lexical resource with a corpus-based distributional semantic resource; (2a) the combination of two resources improves the accuracy of WSD over the accuracy obtained with a single resource; (2b) our approach is comparable to state-of-the-art knowledge-based WSD methods that rely on additional resources such as machine translation systems or web search engines
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions.
the question of whether the combination of two types of lexical resources can lead to a better WSD performance compared to a system that relies only on one type of resource.
the development and evaluation of a simple and effective unsupervised WSD method that is based on two lexical resources only.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our method outperforms all unsupervised WSD approaches that are solely based on knowledge resources.
our method achieves state-of-the-art results for unsupervised sense disambiguated WSD.
our method is competitive with state-of-the-art WSD systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the combination of manually constructed sense-aware lexical networks and distributional semantic models is a promising approach for unsupervised WSD, especially when the latter is not available in a language.
we show the benefits of combining lexical knowledge with distributional semantics for WSD.
the proposed method achieves competitive results with a much simpler architecture and a smaller amount of training data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a combination of manually constructed lexical resources and distributional semantics can yield a WSD system that is as effective as the state-of-the-art hybrid systems.
the combination of two types of lexical resources can improve the quality of sense representations for WSD.
the combination of two lexical resources with complementary strengths can improve the quality of sense representations for WSD, and that this can be accomplished without the use of any training data.
